transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration approx: 45m
Attendees: Daniel (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Maya (BlueCedar - Head ML), Samir (Infra), Dr. Elise (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be incomplete):
Quick scoping to define success criteria for POC focused on latency/throughput SLOs; discuss TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (time-per-token) tradeoffs, p95/p99 targets for chat and batch embedding flows, and measurement plan incl. load shape and KV/prefix caching behavior. Action items: share harness, export traffic, schedule in-lab test window.

Transcript:
[00:00] Daniel (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, do you want to do quick intros?
[00:08] Maya (BlueCedar): sure hi i'm maya lead of ml at bluecedar, we're running models for clinical note summarization and patient triage routing, so latency is pretty important because clinicians expect snappy replies, also PHI is in scope so we'll need private deployment options.
[00:25] Samir (BlueCedar): samir here, infra, i'm on aws and we've got a mixed fleet of g4 and g5 types, we're also evaluating on-prem for a subset of workloads.
[00:33] Dr. Elise (BlueCedar): elise product, main success metric is clinician satisfaction and throughput during morning rounds.
[00:40] Priya (Redwood): awesome, priya here, solutions eng, i'll drive the benchmark plan, daniel will handle commercial and next steps.
[00:47] Daniel (Redwood): cool. quick agenda: align SLOs (ttft vs tpot), define p95/p99 numbers per workload (chat summarize vs bulk embeddings), decide on test harness and traffic profile, and set timeline.

[01:05] Maya: great, question — when you say TTFT, are you measuring server-side only or end-to-end including network? we need to be explicit.
[01:12] Priya: good call, for the POC we'd propose two measurement modes: server-side (Redwood runtime only, measured at ingress to model runtime) and E2E (client to client), we'll capture both. server-side gives us reproducible kernel-level perf; e2e reflects the clinician experience.

[01:30] Samir: for us server-side is the priority because network variability confuses the benchmarking.
[01:36] Daniel: noted. so TTFT definition here: time from request reach to first token emitted by the model runtime. TPOT/time-per-token: median per-token generation after first token when streaming. agreed?
[01:50] Maya: yes. but for our interactive UI we care most about first response p95, then p99.

[02:00] Priya: i'd suggest targets by workload: for interactive summarization (seq len average ~300 tokens) propose TTFT p95 220ms, p99 450ms; TPOT p95 12ms/token, p99 25ms/token. for long-form summarization or batched jobs (embeddings) we propose throughput SLOs as X qps per GPU or p95 latency per batch. (note: numbers are starting points).

[02:28] Maya: those numbers look aggressive, are they for quantized models or fp16? we use a finetuned Llama-like variant.
[02:35] Priya: good point — the recommended test matrix includes model precision (fp16 vs int8/4bit), seq len distribution, and kv cache warm/cold conditions. in our experience int8 with kernel optim can hit the lower TTFTs but with slight quality delta.

[02:55] Samir: our compliance team will likely require private control plane and KMS-backed keys for any PHI. what's the difference for performance between hosted vs private?
[03:04] Daniel: performance on dedicated/private is typically equivalent to hosted when using the same gpu types; the differences are mostly in routing and network overhead. for private on-prem there can be additional latency depending on network topology but we'll capture that in E2E.

[03:20] Dr. Elise: what's TPOT vs throughput in simple terms? our product folks confuse them.
[03:25] Priya: TPOT is per-token time — think of it as the slope once generation starts. throughput is aggregate queries per second for non-streaming batch flows (e.g., embedding pipelines). so a low TPOT helps streaming UX; high throughput matters for nightly batches.

[03:47] Maya: for clinician use case we need TTFT p95 under 300ms ideally and p99 under 700ms. is that feasible?
[03:55] Priya: with a well-tuned inference config (kv caching, prefix cache for repeated prompts, batching carefully limited for interactive routes) yes for fp16 models on g5s we can approach that. we'll validate in the lab.

[04:10] Daniel: let's capture acceptance criteria — i propose the POC pass if: (1) interactive route meets TTFT p95 < 300ms and p99 < 700ms server-side for 95th percentile of your morning-rounds traffic; (2) TPOT p95 < 20ms/token server-side for the same route; (3) embeddings batch job achieves 80% of target throughput with 5% error rate and median latency under your current baseline. any objections?
[04:35] Maya: that map works, though need clarity on how we collect 'morning-rounds traffic' sample.

[04:45] Priya: we'll ask you to provide a 7-day traffic profile CSV — timestamped requests, input length, model variant, and whether streaming was used. we'll synthesize a load shape: 95th percentile concurrency and a 10-minute burst scenario.

[05:00] Samir: what about cache warmup — our system often hits cold-starts after weekend maintenance.
[05:05] Priya: we'll include cold-warm cycles in the harness: run 5 cold starts and capture TTFT distributions, and also measure steady-state after a warmup phase. we'll report cold-start p95/p99 separately.

[05:20] Daniel: on instrumentation, we'll provide a harness that emits server-side logs with millisecond timestamps and token timing hooks. we'll also supply a small client tool to get E2E times. which telemetry do you want ingested into your own observability?
[05:32] Maya: we want metrics in prometheus plus raw CSVs we can drop into our analysis notebooks.

[05:38] Priya: fine, harness will push prometheus summaries + CSV artifacts. we'll include instructions for parsing.

[05:45] Priya: also note we recommend running two benchmark modes: real-time interactive traffic (streaming) and batch (embeddings). for streaming we'll config continuous batching low to keep latency tight; for batch we'll maximize packing for throughput.

[06:00] Maya: how long does Redwood need to run an in-lab test to get statistically significant p99 numbers?
[06:07] Priya: for p99 at 95% confidence on heavy-tailed distributions you'd want a few thousand samples — practically we run 30-60 minutes at target concurrency plus targeted bursts and cold cycles. we'll propose a 2-hour lab run window to be safe.

[06:22] Samir: scheduling note — our infra can open a maintenance window week of 3/16.

[06:28] Daniel: perfect, we'll tentatively plan for in-lab 3/17. Priya will run the tests, we'll share the harness a week earlier.

[06:35] Maya: one more operational question: what if we fail an SLO, what's the remediation for this POC — is it tuning, different model precision, or dedicated nodes?
[06:44] Priya: we'll triage in tiers: 1) tune runtime (batching, kernel flags), 2) try quantization profile or a smaller model variant, 3) recommend dedicated capacity or specialized GPU types. for the POC we'll document recommended changes and re-run the critical tests.

[06:58] Daniel: commercial note — typical POC covers test infra and engineering support for two in-lab runs; we'll share terms after call.

[07:06] Maya: compliance — we need SOC2 docs and a data flow diagram showing PHI handling.
[07:12] Daniel: yes we'll share SOC2 summary and KMS integration docs. for private deployments we can discuss network isolation.

[07:20] Samir: are there any known regressions with finetuned Llama variants? models with large KV sizes sometimes blow up memory during long-seq inference.
[07:29] Priya: true, that's why our runtime supports incremental KV sharding and dynamic memory reclamation; we'll include memory footprint profiling in the report.

[07:40] Dr. Elise: what's the acceptance criteria from product side? beyond latency, do you expect quality checks?
[07:48] Maya: product will look at clinician satisfaction survey and a small eval set of 200 prompts for quality regression.

[07:55] Priya: we'll collect quality checks separate from perf — run prompts and measure token-level differences and a simple BLEU/ROUGE-like metric and flag notable deltas.

[08:05] Daniel: recap of next steps: Redwood to share harness repo + runbook (pri: day after call), BlueCedar to share traffic CSV and sample prompts, schedule in-lab 3/17, Redwood to send SOC2 and SSO/KMS docs, Priya to prepare initial test config with TTFT/TPOT thresholds.

[08:25] Maya: sounds good. can you include default hyperparams you intend to use so we can pre-check?
[08:30] Priya: yes — we'll include model version, precision, batch sizes, prefix cache TTL, kv cache policy, and kernel flags.

[08:38] Daniel: anything else before we close?
[08:41] Samir: small ask — include a quick appendix on how we reproduce results locally if we want to double-check.
[08:47] Priya: will do.

[08:50] Daniel: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed timeline.

[end - meeting ~45m]

Notes on measurement plan (auto art):
- Measurement modes: server-side (ingress->first token + token timing hooks) and E2E (client->client).
- SLOs to validate: TTFT p95/p99, TPOT p95/p99, batch throughput vs baseline, cold-start p95/p99.
- Traffic inputs: 7-day profile + morning-rounds peak, 10-minute burst scenarios, cold-to-warm cycles.
- Test matrix: model precision (fp16, int8), seq len buckets (short <128, med 128-512, long >512), KV warm/cold, concurrency sweep.
- Statistical approach: run 2-hour lab windows per major config; collect >=5000 samples for p99 estimation where possible; report p95/p99 with 95% CI.
- Artifacts delivered: prometheus metrics, raw CSVs with per-request timings, summary spreadsheet with per-config SLO pass/fail, memory profiles, quality regression report.
